column4: Abraham says he has settled descendants in a barren valley by the Sacred House so that they establish prayer, then asks that they receive fruit; household, children, prayer, and provision meet in one appeal.
Fear of failing to deal justly with orphan girls governs whether their guardians may marry them, exposing how entry into the guardian's own household can either protect or exploit the fatherless.
God sends water down in measure and makes it dwell in the earth; measured provision and the source section's س ك ن dwelling root are joined before any household fills a vessel from it.

The ayah uses the withholding root for what prevents hypocrites' expenditures from acceptance, then says they approach prayer lazily and spend reluctantly; worship and the closed hand expose one another.

After Shuayb commands full measure, his people ask whether his prayer orders them to abandon doing whatever they wish with their wealth; the passage explicitly makes prayer accountable for economic conduct.
Those who pray are named as the exception to the human being who becomes withholding when touched by good, providing the bridge from 70:21 to constant prayer and the needy person's known share.
After failure toward the orphan and needy, the passage charges people with devouring inheritance greedily; goods that should sustain the vulnerable are consumed into the powerful household.
Intense love of wealth completes the explanation for 89:17-19: attachment to stored value produces both dishonoring the orphan and refusal to urge feeding.
God found the addressee in need and made him sufficient, placing received provision between remembered orphanhood and the commands not to oppress the orphan or rebuff the asker.
People promise that if God gives them bounty they will give charity and be righteous; 9:76 shows the stocked hand breaking precisely this promise.
The poor emigrants have been expelled from their homes and property; their loss of dwelling and goods supplies the concrete need answered by the household generosity of 59:9.

A secure town receiving abundant provision from every direction denies God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear; plentiful stores become a test whose failure ends in the lack imposed on others.
The command to eat from the harvest and give its due on harvest day puts the grain, the household's consumption, and the recipient's share together before storage can become withholding.
Abraham's visitors are introduced as honored guests, establishing the household stance that his quiet preparation and presentation of food enact in 51:26-27.
The covenant combines establishing prayer, giving alms, and lending God a good loan, directly uniting worship with releasing goods under a promise of return.
The command to establish prayer and give alms is immediately followed by lending God a good loan, placing worship, due provision, and recoverable giving in one instruction.
Household maintainers are identified partly by spending from their wealth, making provision for those within the home a constitutive responsibility rather than an optional favor.
A widow is assigned maintenance for a year without expulsion from the house, joining continued provision to continued shelter when her household guardian is lost.
Divorced women are owed a provision according to recognized good, another household boundary where useful goods must leave the holder's hand as a due.
Divorced women are not to be expelled from their houses during the waiting period, making continued dwelling itself part of the vulnerable household member's protection.
The address to the Prophet's household joins remaining within the houses with establishing prayer and giving alms, bringing domestic space, worship, and material duty into one frame.
Wealth and children are declared a test immediately before the commands to resist greed and spend, making the household's dependents and stores the very site of moral trial.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way are warned, turning retained household wealth into an explicit instance of stored usefulness denied circulation.
The hoarded metal is heated and used to brand its owners, so the substance kept back becomes the instrument that exposes and punishes withholding.

Some entrusted with a great sum return it, while another will not return even a single coin unless persistently pressed; the ayah tests the section's expectation that a borrowed household item normally comes back.
A debtor in hardship must receive time, and remitting the debt is better; this sets compassion above the lender's expectation of return when the borrower truly cannot restore what was lent.
Household dependents seeking a contract for freedom are to receive some of the wealth God gave the householder, directing divinely supplied property toward the dependent's release.
Charity is voided by reminders, injury, and spending to be seen by people; provision leaving the hand must differ inwardly from the surah's display-oriented worship.
Concealed charity delivered to the poor is called better for the giver, providing the positive counterpart to public display while keeping the needy recipient in view.
Those who spend their wealth to be seen by people are condemned, clarifying that a visible gift can reproduce the same display that empties prayer of care.

Israel asks to exchange one food for a list of ordinary crops, and misery is then laid upon them; food and the س ك ن family's maskanah branch meet here in a different sense from settled household shelter.
Maskanah is laid upon the condemned people, using the section's س ك ن family for abjection rather than dwelling or household provision and thus marking a secondary semantic boundary.
God holds the treasuries of all things and sends each down only in known measure, scaling the stocked shelf and measured container into a governed economy of provision.
If provision were expanded without limit people would transgress, so God sends it by measure; the ayah distinguishes measured supply from both deficient giving and destructive excess.
Water is sent from heaven in due measure and revives dead land, a remote but concrete source for the water eventually carried in the section's loanable bucket.
God is the Provider and possessor of firm power, completing 51:57's statement that He seeks no provision or feeding and grounding human food in received supply.
People are commanded to spend before death makes them beg for a delay in which to give charity, exposing how the supposedly postponable small good becomes irretrievable.
The righteous spend in both ease and hardship, refusing to turn a less-than-full household into a blanket excuse for withholding.
A divorced woman is to receive a gift according to the giver's means and recognized good, a measured household transfer that preserves care at separation.
Even a deed the weight of a mustard seed is brought into the just balance, giving the section's tiny, easy kindness a precise moral weight.
Luqman tells his son that even a mustard-seed-sized deed hidden in rock will be brought forth by God, joining household instruction of a child with the visibility of the smallest act.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, completing 99:7's assurance that a tiny good matters and applying the same scale to withholding it.
No expenditure, small or large, goes unrecorded, explicitly protecting the moral significance of the section's slight and easy contribution.
The record omits neither a small thing nor a great one, a general but specific answer to the belief that refusal of a trivial household aid is beneath account.
A cup from a flowing spring is passed around among the blessed, making circulation rather than possession the action of the vessel.
Everlasting youths circulate among the blessed, supplying the act of passing that belongs to the cups and pitchers named in 56:18.
The human being is told to look at his food, opening a sequence that traces what fills the household dish back through water, earth, and grain.
God pours water abundantly, the first material contribution to the food whose source the eater is commanded to inspect.
God splits the earth open, continuing the production chain that precedes any grain poured into a domestic measure.
Grain is made to grow from the opened earth, directly supplying the substance the section pictures settling into a shaken measure.
The crops are provision for people and their livestock, concluding that the entire food sequence is supplied benefit rather than self-created household property.
Joseph orders seven years of cultivation and tells the people to leave grain in its ears except the little they eat, giving a concrete scene of food retained for future household survival.
Seven hard years will consume what was stored except a little kept in reserve, marking necessary preservation as a boundary distinct from miserly withholding.
People must spend from that over which God made them successors, reframing the objects and provisions inside the house as entrusted holdings.

The people of the Fire ask for water or some of God's provision and are refused because those gifts are forbidden to them, an eschatological boundary where refusal is judgment rather than household miserliness.
Adam and his spouse are told to dwell in the Garden and eat freely from it, joining settled household companionship to abundant accessible food.
The repeated command has Adam and his spouse dwell in the Garden and eat wherever they wish, another direct coupling of س ك ن dwelling and provision.
God guarantees every creature's provision and knows its settled place and repository, placing sustenance, dwelling, and storage within one divine account.
Many creatures do not carry their own provision, yet God provides for them and for people; fear of an unstocked future is not proof that the hand must remain closed.
The separated boy Joseph is sold for a few coins and treated as of little value, showing the cruel reversal in which the vulnerable child, rather than a utensil, becomes the cheap disposable thing.
The Egyptian buyer tells his wife to honor the boy's lodging and considers adopting him, reversing expulsion by receiving a separated child into the home.
After helping strangers at the well, Moses withdraws to shade and tells God he is in need of whatever good is sent, voicing the needy asker's dependence without demanding from people.
One woman then invites Moses to her household so her father can repay his help, moving the needy traveler from an open well toward shelter and recompense.
The hypocrites are told that spending willingly or unwillingly will not be accepted, establishing the inward boundary for the reluctant expenditure diagnosed with lazy prayer in 9:54.
Night is made for people to rest in, repeating the section's س ك ن root-family idea of repose without itself depicting a house or material provision.
Night is made so people may rest in it, a repeated repose sense that faintly clarifies why a dwelling and its sustaining goods share the section's root-family image.
God makes night for rest and day for sight, another repeated non-household use of the repose underlying the section's س ك ن associations.
